text: The churn API works on the machine where you built it. That is exactly the problem. A saved model is sensitive to the exact versions of Python, scikit-learn, NumPy, and pandas it was trained with, and the server that runs it is not your laptop. Docker packages the service, its libraries, and the model file into one image that runs the same way everywhere.
A quick honesty note: Docker was not installed where this lesson was written, so the Dockerfile was not built here. It follows Docker's and FastAPI's official guidance.

Start from pinned requirements: the exact versions from training. Here is why. We asked pip for scikit-learn one point one point two on Python three point eleven, and it refused. On Python three point ten it found a match. So the base image must be Python three point ten slim, not whatever is newest.
The Dockerfile begins with that base image, copies only the requirements file, and installs from it. Because Docker caches layers, this slow step is reused until your requirements change.

Then we create a non-root user, copy the app and the models folder, and start uvicorn in exec form, bound to zero dot zero dot zero dot zero, since the default address is unreachable from outside the container.

To use it, build the image with a tag that carries the model version, run it with the port published, and call the health endpoint. Then send the same predict request as before and compare the answer with your local server.

A few model-specific choices. Baking the model into the image ties one model version to one image tag, which is simple and traceable. Keep training tools and data out of the serving image. And use one server process per container, letting the platform handle replication.
